title: Emergency IO Surge Recovery and Safe Deploy Checklist (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working draft checklist and post-incident notes for a class of infra incidents we keep seeing around sustained IO / GPU device thrashing that cause 1) JVM/worker stalls, 2) degraded throughput on serving clusters, and 3) noisy autoscaler reactions. The intent: give on-call a compact, pragmatic set of steps to stabilize traffic, get capacity back, and capture data for later replacement/PSA.

Scope / when to use this doc:
- Tier-1 production incidents where inference tail latency or request failures spike across multiple nodes and correlate with accelerator device errors, PCIe errors, or host IO saturation.
- Not intended for single-container OOMs or routine pod restarts; those use the normal k8s pod remediation playbook.

High-level strategy (triage flow):
1) Stop the bleeding: reduce incoming load, enable fallback routing (model variants/CPU pool), and pause non-essential jobs.
2) Contain the blast radius: cordon and drain suspect nodes in small batches, avoid mass-evacuations without capacity plan.
3) Patch-up capacity: inject reserve nodes or reroute to Dedicated/hosted pools, or relax autoscaler cooldowns.
4) Replace hardware: escalate physical GPU replacement (if needed) using hardware ops checklist.
5) Recover and validate: confirm KV cache warmup, latency percentiles, and end-to-end correctness with canary traffic.

Detection signals to watch (alerts that should route to SRE oncall):
- node_exporter: disk_io_utilization > 85% sustained for 5m across N nodes
- dmesg / journal: repeated NVMe/PCIe errors or GPU driver warnings
- kubelet: pod eviction / OOM series + Kubelet drain timeouts
- serving metrics: 99th p95/p99 latency spikes + 5xx rate increase by >3x
- autoscaler: scale-up thrash (add/remove within cooldown)
- telemetry: errors referencing device X (nvidia-smi errors, driver timeouts)

Immediate on-call checklist (first 15 minutes):
- Acknowledge incident and ping #sre-oncall + service owner in Slack.
- POST mortem stub: create INC ticket (link in metadata).
- Reduce incoming traffic: flip emergency-rate-limit route or apply global ingress throttle (gateway: /emergency/ratelimit).
- Switch critical traffic to fallback model family or cheaper CPU workers: routing flag "model.fallback=enabled" via the routing service.
- Disable batch accumulation in serving runtime to reduce memory pressure: set TEMP_CONFIG=batch.window_ms=0 for affected model routes.
- Snapshot logs and package: nvidia-smi -q, dmesg | tail -n 200, journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 > /tmp/incident-logs.tar.gz and upload to INC ticket.

Node assessment and isolation (safe pattern):
- Do NOT cordon >3 nodes at once in a single AZ unless you have >30% spare capacity.
- Prioritize nodes with: repeated device errors, high PCIe/category errors, or extended kubelet restarts.
Step-by-step:
1) Mark node unschedulable: kubectl cordon <node>  # note timestamp
2) Evict only serving pods gracefully: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m --pod-selector="app=redwood-serving"
   - If drain hangs >5m: kill long-lived acceleration containers (careful).
   - If eviction fails due to local data: annotate pod with emergency-evict=true and force-delete (last resort).
3) Monitor cluster capacity while draining using the console: expected CPU/GPU headroom > 10% after each drain action.
4) If headroom would drop below threshold, STOP draining and trigger capacity add step below.

Temporary routing and capacity add (fast path):
- Use dedicated spare pool (reserved capacity) if available: route traffic with tag route.cluster=dedicated-spare.
- If no spare pool: increase node pool desired count via cluster autoscaler override: terraform-managed override or cloud console API. Coordinate with infra oncall for provider quota checks.
- For immediate relief, enable cross-zone routing to avoid AZ hot spots: routing.policy=allow-cross-az for 30m.

GPU device swap / hardware ops (when node shows persistent device failure):
- Escalate to hardware-ops (pager: Diego A.) and include node name, serial, dmesg excerpt, and last successful workload time.
- If doing physical replacement on-site or via cloud provider RMA, follow the hardware ops acceptance checklist: power cycle, reseat accelerators, run driver health probes, run a smoke inference job at low qps, verify nv_peer_mem and MIG configs.
- Post-swap verification steps: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,mig.mode.current --format=csv, run small synthetic generator (10 qps) with known prompt set, confirm latency < 2x baseline p95 and 0 errors.

Cluster recovery and validation (post-stabilization):
- Gradually re-enable batching, revert TEMP_CONFIG changes, and monitor token-level cost/latency for regressions.
- Run a smoke canary suite: 1000 requests across critical routes, measure correctness ratio and p95 latency.
- Warm KV/prefix cache: replay a curated list of recent high-traffic prefixes to the warmed nodes to minimize cold-token penalty.
- Check model variant fallbacks and ensure traffic is pinned back to primary model versions using rollout controller.

Observability capture (what to collect into the incident ticket):
- Graph snapshots of latency, error-rate, autoscaler events, and per-node device error counts for the 1h before/after.
- Logs: kubelet, container runtime, dmesg, kernel messages, driver logs (nvidia/rocm).
- Pod placement map and shard mapping before and after drains.
- Batch and KV cache metrics.

Post-incident follow-ups (owner assignments):
- Root cause hypothesis: assign to eng-serving-runtime for kernel/driver root cause or infra for networking/PCIe fabric.
- Action item: add a 2-node spare pool in each AZ (ticket INFRA-RESERVE-2025). Owner: Linh Tran.
- Action item: add device-level alerting for repeated ECC errors (Owner: Priya).
- Action item: bake a graceful force-evict utility into kube tooling to avoid manual deletions (Owner: Ethan).

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self):
- Should we expose a single-button global "emergency-throttle" in the console linked to an incident ticket? work with product-console.
- How quickly can Dedicated pools absorb sustained traffic for long-running incidents (cost ops impact)? Need runbook for billing/approval.
- Evaluate whether autoscaler cooldowns are too short; currently 90s, consider 5m for GPU pools.

Known gotchas and cautionary notes:
- Removing the node too fast without verifying KV warmup can cause repeated cold-start latency spikes and a second outage.
- Force-deleting pods can orphan local caches and cause correctness issues; avoid unless the business impact justifies it.
- Cross-AZ routing temporarily increases tail latency due to network hops; only use until core nodes recover.

Quick recovery checklist (TL;DR):
1) Throttle ingress + enable fallback model family.
2) Cordon 1 node at a time, drain serving pods only.
3) If headroom < threshold: trigger capacity add (dedicated spare or autoscaler override).
4) Replace/repair GPU if device errors persist; run smoke tests.
5) Canary traffic, warm caches, revert temp config changes.
6) Populate incident ticket with artifacts and assign postmortem owners.

Appendix: useful commands and scripts
- Collect logs: /usr/local/bin/collect-device-diagnostics.sh <node>  # uploads tarball to incident ticket
- Force drain helper: kubectl drain <node> --pod-selector=app=redwood-serving --grace-period=30 --force --timeout=5m  # only if approved by eng-sre lead
- Re-route to dedicated spare: curl -X POST https://routing.internal/api/v1/route-override -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","target":"dedicated-spare"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ROUTE_TOKEN'

Notes: this is intentionally conversational and contains heuristics — keep it short and practical. We'll expand into separate hardware-ops and autoscaler-runbooks after the next incident postmortem.

Last edited by Priya Narayanan on 2025-02-08.
